title: Characterization of human aquaporin protein-protein interactions using microscale thermophoresis
author: Al-Jubair, Steffen, et al.

steps.title: Fit binding curve
steps.instruction: Use an appropriate curve‑fitting program and the one‑to‑one binding equation to determine the dissociation constant (Kd) by plotting normalized fluorescence (Fnorm) against ligand concentration. Apply the equation y = S1 + (S2−S1)·(LFree/(LFree+KD)), where LFree = 0.5·(LTot−PTot−KD) + 0.25·√[(KD+PTot−LTot)² + 4·LTot·KD]. Define S1 and S2 as the signals of the unbound and bound forms, respectively; LTot as the total concentration of unlabeled protein (AQP); PTot as the total concentration of the labeled protein; and KD as the dissociation constant.

substeps.instruction: Enter the measured Fnorm values and corresponding ligand concentrations into the software.
Select the provided binding equation and fit the data to obtain KD.
Record the fitted parameters (S1, S2, KD) for further analysis.

steps.title: Analyze replicates
steps.instruction: Perform statistical analysis using the three independently prepared dilution series to assess reproducibility and calculate confidence intervals for the binding affinity.

description: Microscale thermophoresis (MST) is based on the principle that the movement of molecules in a thermal gradient depends on their size, charge, and solvation shell. It has the advantage of being fully compatible with a range of buffer conditions, including the presence of detergents, as well as low sample consumption (Jerabek-Willemsen et al., 2011). For these reasons, MST is particularly well suited for studying protein-protein interactions involving membrane proteins. Below we describe a protocol that we routinely use for studying the interaction between full-length human AQPs and a soluble interaction partner.
